Hello developers,

I just finished playing your game on the Switch, and I immediately bought the Steam version to add to my library. The game's atmosphere and narrative pacing really drew me in, and the background music was perfectly fitting. Because of this, I'm happy to leave a positive review, though it also left me with higher expectations.

 [spoiler]
The game is about four hours long, and playing it felt more like watching a movie. However, as a game, it offered too few choices for the player. During my play through, I tried to deliberately not answer the supervisor's calls or even pretended to be a 'good kid' to see if there was a way to betray HAL. But the game didn't give me any more options. I believe that in an interactive story game, player choices and their consequences are its true charm and what keeps players engaged.
The bomb disposal segment really stood out. I felt a strong sense of immersion and genuinely enjoyed being able to help someone. It's a shame that, probably due to the game's length, such a brilliant sequence only happened once.
The core puzzle was very cleverly designed, and its reveal was absolutely an adrenaline rush. I completely understand what you, as developers, wanted players to feel with that ending—the horror, the profound sense of melancholy, the sadness for the characters, and the lingering regret that a bigger enemy wasn't truly dealt with. However, even after experiencing all that, I still wished players could help the characters achieve a good ending. I truly love these characters.
Overall, this is a fantastic game! I really hope to play more from you in the future!
[/spoiler]

The Operator – 8/10 – A Tense and Captivating Dive into Espionage

The Operator is a stealth-driven, psychological thriller that plunges players into the shadowy world of covert operations, high-stakes intelligence, and moral ambiguity. With an engaging narrative and a compelling atmosphere, it combines tactical gameplay with deep narrative exploration, offering a gripping experience for fans of espionage games. While it may not reinvent the wheel, The Operator does a great job of delivering a tightly-paced, immersive story that keeps you on the edge of your seat.

In The Operator, you play as a field agent working for a secretive government agency, tasked with handling covert missions that blur the lines between right and wrong. The game is heavy on stealth and strategy, as you navigate through a series of complex scenarios—whether infiltrating a heavily guarded facility, gathering intelligence, or neutralizing a threat. The gameplay is tense and slow-paced, with an emphasis on thinking ahead, blending in with your surroundings, and making choices that can lead to either success or failure. It’s all about staying unseen, listening for clues, and using your limited resources wisely. The tension constantly builds as you wonder if you’ll be caught or if the consequences of your decisions will haunt you later on.

The game’s mechanics are simple but effective. You don’t have a full arsenal at your disposal like in many action-heavy titles, and that’s part of the charm. The focus here is on patience, strategy, and managing the few tools you have, whether it’s a silenced pistol or hacking equipment. The difficulty comes not from constant firefights but from the challenge of navigating through dangerous environments, avoiding detection, and managing the relationships and choices you make along the way.

One of The Operator’s strongest points is its atmosphere. The game does an excellent job of crafting a sense of isolation and tension, using sound design, lighting, and environment to its advantage. The dark, minimalist environments add to the oppressive mood, and the voice acting and soundtrack complement the sense of secrecy and paranoia that runs throughout the game. You always feel like you’re being watched, and every decision could push you deeper into the world of shadowy operatives and untrustworthy allies.

The narrative is intriguing and filled with twists, as you’ll often have to decide whether to follow orders or act according to your own moral compass. The story doesn’t just follow the usual espionage tropes—it explores themes of trust, betrayal, and the emotional toll of being part of a covert operation. The characters you meet, especially the ones you interact with the most, are well-written and add layers of complexity to the plot. The game gives you enough room to shape your own interpretation of events, but it doesn’t shy away from showing the darker consequences of a life lived in secrecy.

However, The Operator does have its shortcomings. The stealth mechanics, while solid, can feel repetitive at times, especially in the later levels where the pacing slows down significantly. There are also a few technical hiccups, like occasional AI pathfinding issues or moments when the game’s visuals don’t quite match the level of detail of the environments. Some players may also find the slower pace a bit tedious, particularly if they’re expecting a more action-packed experience.

8/10 – A Solid, Tense Espionage Experience
The Operator is a highly effective stealth game that delivers a tense, engaging experience for anyone who loves espionage narratives. While its mechanics might feel repetitive in certain sections, the atmosphere, story, and the moral complexity of the choices you make keep it captivating throughout. The game’s slow pace and emphasis on stealth give it a unique edge in a genre often dominated by faster-paced action. If you’re a fan of games that require patience and strategic thinking, The Operator will keep you hooked. It might not be perfect, but it’s a well-executed, atmospheric title that leaves a lasting impression.

review_text_raw:
The Operator, developed by Bureau 81 and published by Bureau 81 together with indienova, is a tightly focused narrative puzzle game that transforms the quiet, procedural work of intelligence analysis into a tense and engaging thriller. Rather than placing players in the role of an action hero or field agent, the game casts them as a desk-bound operator, someone whose power comes not from physical presence but from information, observation, and deduction. This shift in perspective defines the entire experience, creating a game that feels intimate, cerebral, and deliberately restrained.

You play as Evan Tanner, a newly recruited operator working for the fictional Federal Department of Intelligence. Your job is to support agents in the field by analysing data, processing evidence, and drawing connections that others might miss. The game unfolds almost entirely through Evan’s workstation, presented as a simulated computer desktop filled with databases, analysis tools, messaging systems, and case files. This interface-driven approach immediately sets the tone: instead of cinematic spectacle, The Operator relies on immersion through routine, making the player feel like they are genuinely sitting at a government terminal late at night, piecing together fragments of truth.

Gameplay revolves around solving a series of cases that gradually escalate in complexity and importance. Early tasks feel procedural—identifying suspects, tracing movements, or cross-referencing records—but as the story unfolds, patterns begin to emerge and the stakes rise. Players are required to closely read documents, examine photos and videos, search databases, and interpret subtle clues hidden in plain sight. The puzzles reward attentiveness and logical reasoning, often asking players to synthesize information from multiple sources rather than relying on a single obvious answer. When a breakthrough occurs, it feels earned, the result of careful thought rather than trial and error.

As the narrative progresses, the game shifts from isolated casework into a broader conspiracy. A mysterious hacker begins to interfere with FDI systems, raising questions about surveillance, authority, and the reliability of the information you’re working with. This transition adds narrative tension without abandoning the game’s grounded tone. The story remains largely linear, but it is effectively paced, allowing suspense to build gradually as seemingly unrelated assignments reveal deeper connections. Dialogue and character interactions are understated, delivered through calls, messages, and system prompts rather than dramatic cutscenes, which reinforces the feeling that you are always working behind the scenes.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is how convincingly it uses its interface as both a storytelling and gameplay tool. Every window, search bar, and analysis program feels purposeful, and learning how to use these tools becomes part of the experience. While some mechanics are simplified or exaggerated for gameplay purposes, they remain believable within the fiction, maintaining immersion. The design encourages players to slow down, double-check assumptions, and think critically—mistakes often stem from overlooking details rather than misunderstanding mechanics.

Visually, The Operator embraces a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic inspired by older operating systems and institutional software. The interface is dense but readable, intentionally lacking visual flair in favor of authenticity. This design choice may feel dry to some players, but it suits the game’s themes perfectly, emphasizing bureaucracy, control, and the monotony of surveillance work. Subtle audio cues, ambient hums, and restrained music enhance tension without distracting from concentration, allowing the player’s focus to remain on the task at hand.

In terms of pacing, the game strikes a careful balance. It is compact, typically completed in a handful of hours, but it avoids feeling rushed. Each case builds naturally on the last, and the increasing narrative weight keeps momentum strong. The linear structure limits replayability, as choices rarely branch into significantly different outcomes, but this also allows the developers to maintain tight narrative control and deliver a coherent, focused story without filler.

Community reception reflects appreciation for the game’s originality and execution. Players who enjoy detective work, mystery narratives, and “games on a computer” style experiences frequently praise its atmosphere and puzzle design. Criticism tends to focus on its short length, limited player agency, and occasional moments where immersion is broken by game-like constraints. Even so, these issues rarely overshadow the strengths of the experience, particularly for players aligned with its intended audience.

Taken as a whole, The Operator is a confident and distinctive narrative puzzle game that finds tension in observation rather than action. It succeeds by committing fully to its premise, turning data analysis and desk work into compelling gameplay through thoughtful design and strong thematic focus. While it may not appeal to players seeking open-ended systems or high replay value, it offers a memorable, tightly constructed experience for those who enjoy slow-burn storytelling, logical deduction, and the quiet unease of uncovering truths from behind a screen.

Rating: 9/10

review_text_raw:
My experience with The Operator can be summed up as follows: great presentation, limited investigation.  It's a  game that looks sharp, feels polished, and tells a story that is rather entertaining, yet never quite trusts you enough to truly investigate it on your own. I enjoyed my time with it. I just kept wishing it would let me off the leash.

The production is slick from top to bottom. The performances sell the drama, and the narrative momentum keeps you moving even when a few plot holes start to peek through if you linger too long on the details. It is a fun story. It just is not a particularly demanding one.

Let’s be clear about something. This is not really an investigation game.

You are deliberately guided from one beat to the next with little room to wander or hope oiff the beaten path. That keeps the pacing tight, sure, but it also strips away the thrill of deduction that hallmarks great detective games . No alternate paths, no clever lateral thinking moments, no opportunities to feel like you outsmarted the system. Outside of one genuinely challenging, spoiler free sequence that actually made me pause and think, most of the puzzles feel straightforward and simple to resolve.

And then there is the ending. I assumed I had stumbled into the Bad Ending because of something I had done wrong, only to realize that this was simply... the finish. And I figured it was disappointing.

This game didn't scratch my detective game itch. I love having my detective instincts tested. I enjoy piecing together clues and trusting my logic to guide me. I wanted more depth, more resistance. That said, for someone easing into detective style games for the first time, this is an excellent starting point. As long as you're picking it up on sale.

review_text_raw:
Overall, I adored this game.  I struggle with this next phrase because i don't fully mean it and understand why it is the way it is... but I'm glad I bought it on sale and not full price as it's not quite worth the full price.  I mostly say this due to game length and lack of choice in endings.  I took a look and it looks like this might be a first time game from this dev, who I'm guessing is solo or very small which is VERY exciting to see if this is their freshman showing.

Things I LOVED:
-Dynamic story telling.  There was a clear storyline running through from start to finish.  Not overly convoluted, not too cliche or simple.  Were the twists a little predictable?  Maybe a few.  But that didn't take away from the impact when they hit anyway.  The pacing of those drops were excellently done.
-Style was lovely.  I REALLY dug the overall look of the game.  The various tools you got to us, the puzzles you go to solve... all from a single terminal.  It made me think of a hacking game from the early 00s of gaming sites that I loved to play over and over.
-The voice acting was excellent.  Really stellar work.
-The game itself.  It's just really enjoyable.  It was well paced, the mystery was fun, the story was easy to follow, the puzzles were a bit easy but a few had some real challenges in there.  One puzzle was a bit too much of a lateral thinking puzzle, BUT that was one of the best twists of the whole game so I can overlook it. 

Things I wish were different (not bad, just things I wanted more of):
-it's far too short.  It took me about 4 hours to complete and that was going very slow and taking my time, looking at my phone a lot and doing a few other things at the same time. (thanks ADHD)  The story telling and plot that the game is driving could easily have been a full scale game.  And I'd pay good money for it, too.  This is top notch story telling from a new dev and I hope we see more.
-Lack of use of cool tools.  You're introduced to several cool mini puzzles throughout the game like a car analyzer, a bomb diffuser, and chemical component analyzer.  All of them have robust rules and options with them.  And they're all used only once.  You gave us so many cool toys.. let us play with them!!
-No story diversity with a [spoiler] really weak and bad ending [/spoiler].  While the story they have given is lovely, your choices don't matter.  There is just that ending.  I wanted more options, i wanted to affect the story with how i played and wanted the game reward cleverness (i.e. if you found a certain name on a certain list before you were told to.)

All that being said, if you like mystery games, if you like hack style games, this is a great choice.  I am very excited to see what this dev does in the future.  If this is their first showing, we are in for some real gems in the future!!

review_text_raw:
*Well made thriller, intriguing story, albeit flawed and very short*

The Operator has you play as Evan Tanner, the titular operator of the fictional FDI. Your task is to sit behind a computer and conduct forensic inestigations with state-of-the-art tools to help your colleagues in the field. 
You quickly become part of a major conspiracy and need to uncover the secrets of a series of missing cases and murders.

I did enjoy my time with the games but it has a fair amount of shortcomings, my main issues being the short length and abrupt ending.

The game mainly involves you getting sent files such as video feeds by FDI agents that you need to sleuth through to uncover important information such as the ID of a suspect. The tasks are pretty varied to keep it from getting stale. However, the game does not flesh out the gameplay. Many tasks are done only once, making it feel fairly shallow. 

The main focus is clearly the story. It is intriguing and does enough to keep you hooked. 
The voice actors do a good job portraying their characters, although they can feel underdeveloped. While I did enjoy it for the most part, it felt rushed to me. The already fast pacing picks up at the end, and then the game just ends, leaving many unanswered questions. The game also teases multiple endings by giving you the illusion of choices throughout the story, but there is only a singular storyline.

The presentation is well done and immersive thanks to the visuals and sound design. The soundtrack also does a good job accompanying the story by kicking in at important beats.

Tl;Dr: The Operator is an absolute gem and probably one of my favorite gaming experiences this year. It nails its atmosphere and story, with a few small quirks holding it back from perfection.

[h1] What I Loved [/h1]
[h3]The Layout:[/h3] The environments and flow are super well-designed. You’re never lost, but there’s enough to explore to keep things interesting.

[h3]Subtle 90s Vibes:[/h3] The aesthetic is on point—just the right touch of nostalgia without feeling overdone. If you love that slightly grainy, retro tech vibe, you’ll be right at home.

[h3]UI:[/h3] Clean, simple, and fits the tone perfectly. You never feel like you’re fighting the menus, which is always a win.

[h3]Voice Acting:[/h3] Honestly, top-tier. The performances are so natural, and they add so much depth to the story.
Pacing: The game knows when to keep things moving and when to let moments breathe. It’s a tight, well-paced experience.

[h3]The Ending:[/h3] I won’t spoil anything, but wow—it sticks the landing. One of those endings that makes you sit there for a second and just think, wish for more but grow more satisfied with what (little) you know.

[h1]What I Didn’t Love[/h1]

[h3]No Narrative Skip:[/h3] This is a big one for achievement hunters. If you miss something, you’ll have to sit through all the dialogue again, which can get frustrating.

[h3]No Replay Value:[/h3] They’re upfront about this, but I still think it’s a shame. The world and story are so good that even small additions—alternate choices or alternating riddles ([spoiler]Read: Bomb[/spoiler]) or hidden paths—would’ve added a lot.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]
If you’re into story-driven games with a great atmosphere, The Operator is 100% worth your time. It’s short, sweet, and delivers an experience that sticks with you. Sure, it’s a one-and-done kind of deal, but honestly, it’s so good while it lasts that I didn’t mind too much.

Wow this was pretty incredible! I was expecting a sort of Papers Please esque game but that you are a sort of detective, but it was way more than that. Especially when it comes to the story, which was surprisingly the biggest focus of this game. What was great though was that the story was really good and took a lot of twists and turns. Feels like you are playing through a great movie actually, but rather in a pacing way and not in the way where you just look at custcenes or whatever. Just trying to go through the different cases is also super satisfying and there is actually a surprising amount of variety in your different methods. Sure, you can make different choices and such I think (but I do not think the narrative at large can change?), but the actual cases do not seem to change. I would have hoped for some sort of an "endless mode" where cases would be randomly generated to an extent. The gameplay is just so cool and engaging and I think it is a shame that there is not more of it, even though I thouroughly enjoyed the game.

Super impressed with the game and totally recommend it if you like conspiracies, detective work, Papers Please and great stories!

A short game that puts you in the chair of a government operator working remotely to aid agents and uncover a mystery.

This game is dripping with immersion, from sound to mechanics. The operator PC is an excellent tool in both storytelling and in making you feel like you're operating the computer yourself. Although not too in-depth, what it does do with the concept it succeeds - so much so that I honestly wish this was a much longer detective-style game that allowed you to do more missions, but what it does have is enough for the story.
When it comes to the story, it's pretty good. It's a nice blend of suspense and mystery that feels like an interactive spy thriller with a more grounded feel. The voice-acting is excellent with a believable quality to it, and the pacing/presentation is excellently done. There's not much in replayability, but I think the story does a great enough job nonetheless.

When it comes to achievements/completion, it's good. Some of the achievements are missable and require very specific actions - though nothing so crazy that you feel the need to replay it just to get it.

Overall I really do recommend this game. If you want a short and effective story with some good investigative elements, I think this is worth getting.

What an amazing experience this game is.
A well written story with excellent pacing, and also very good voice acting. It features amazing sound design that really cements the suspense and excitement that this game portrays so well.

The gameplay is simplistic, but shows a lot of thought and care in its design.
You play with a virtual tabletop where you'll navigate files, folders and the chat-system you utilise to communicate with agents. You'll be scanning pictures and videos for details, and cross-check data with the company database that lists any person you can identify with a full name or via face recognition, among other things...

As I finished the game I was filled with a hunger for more. And the systems implemented in this game leaves nigh limitless potential for future projects based on the same concept. I loved every second playing this game, and I hope to see more from this developer in the future.
